### **Cycle 111 Newsroom Continuity Brief**

---

### **1. West Oakland's Month-Ten Money Clears the Desk. What Happens on the Street Is Not on the Ledger.**

* **Prior Events & Promises:**  
  * The **West Oakland Stabilization Fund** was proposed by **Mayor Avery Santana** and passed in **Cycle 78** on a narrow **6–3 City Council vote** (with Councilmembers **Ramon Vega** voting yes, **Leonard Tran** voting no, and **Elliott Crane** voting yes remotely) [1, 2].  
  * Sized with a total envelope of **\$28 million**, the initiative reached its ninth month of active disbursement in **Cycle 110**, logging **\$400,000 approved for Month-Nine** and achieving a **23-day average processing window** [1, 3, 4].  
  * The ledger recorded **\$81,188 disbursed in direct household grants** through Cycle 109, carrying **\$23 million remaining** in reserve [1, 3].  
* **Named Citizens, Officials & Institutions:**  
  * **Marcus Webb** (Finance Committee): Reported to auditors that **79 households have been stabilized in nine months** with direct checks in hand before displacement notices arrived [4].  
  * **Mayor Avery Santana**: Frame: *"Nine months in, we're proving that relief without bureaucracy keeps neighbors in their neighborhoods"* [5].  
  * **Brenda Okoro** (Executive Leadership): Frame: *"targeted relief that flows to tenants before displacement does"* [5].  
  * **Denise Carter** (District 1 Councilmember): Frame: *"When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving"* [6].  
  * **Daniel Cloak** (bakery worker), **Irene Fay** (coffee shop barista), **Darius Clark** (bakery regular), and **Elena Patel** (resident): Reported four weeks into implementation that residents were still watching and waiting, seeing zero visible financial arrival or impact on their blocks [7-11].  
* **Direct Published Facts vs. Inferences:**  
  * **Direct Published Fact:** Month-Nine approved \$400,000 at a 23-day processing pace, stabilizing 79 households on paper with \$23 million remaining [1, 4]. **Month-Ten disbursement review is scheduled for Cycle 111** [12].  
  * **Analytical Inference & Unresolved Storyline:** Editor **Mags Corliss** highlights an unresolved arithmetic discrepancy between the \$28 million initial envelope, \$81,188 in disbursed household grants, and \$23 million remaining [3]. The core unresolved storyline entering Cycle 111 is whether the Month-Ten review reconciles the ledger figures and accelerates cash delivery to residents before commercial displacement outpaces public aid [12].

---

### **2. The Port Got Louder. Down the Block, the Ledger Barely Moved.**

* **Prior Events & Industrial/Tech Expansion:**  
  * Private corporate capital expanded along West Oakland's business corridor through **Oakmesh Systems**, **Civis Systems** (founded by **Elias Varek**), and **Coastline Construction** (managing partner **Desmond Achebe**), alongside **Mariner Construction** and **Northgate Construction** [13-15].  
* **Named Personnel & Field Witnesses:**  
  * **Enzo Walker** (Oakmesh plumber): Reported spending half his working hours fixing plumbing in newly erected buildings that didn't exist a year ago [13-15]. Quoted: *"The money's there, sure, but it's not sticking around here... We're all just trying to keep the water running while the city builds over us"* [13, 15].  
  * **Dom Will** (Oakmesh machine learning engineer): Stated Oakmesh is *"building something real... Marcus keeps us focused on civic impact, not just profit"* [13, 16].  
  * **Sam Fazio** (Civis Systems digital twin architect): Described growth as a *"shared project"* alongside founder **Elias Varek** and drone fleet coordinator **Maurice Franklin** [13, 15, 17].  
* **Direct Published Facts vs. Inferences:**  
  * **Direct Published Fact:** Corporate tech, drone fleet, and commercial construction firms are actively building and hiring along West Oakland's business lane [14-16].  
  * **Analytical Inference & Unresolved Storyline:** Mags Corliss and reporter **Jordan Velez** infer that private money arrives fast and visible, while public municipal investment fails to settle onto the surrounding block [13, 17]. The unresolved storyline entering Cycle 111 is whether local commercial growth translates into lasting neighborhood infrastructure benefits or leaves adjacent streets behind [17].

---

### **3. Chinatown's Line Is Shorter Than Its Count**

* **Prior Events & Organized Care Ledger:**  
  * **Maria Keen’s** culture audit revealed that on Telegraph Avenue, the **Temescal Islamic Center Food Pantry** (standing since **Cycle 83**) remains the **single listed program of organized care** on the official record [18-20].  
  * **Demographic Count:** This single food pantry program holds the line for a rising resident count of **311 kids**, **2,106 working adults**, and **294 seniors** [18, 20, 21].  
  * **Corridor & Transit Context:** In Cycle 110, transit reporter **Trevor Shimizu** noted that Lake Merritt transit shifts coincided with events in Lake Merritt and Chinatown, directly affecting foot traffic and local worker connections [22, 23].  
* **Direct Published Facts vs. Inferences:**  
  * **Direct Published Fact:** Official municipal ledgers list only one organized care program serving hundreds of new residents across the corridor [18-20].  
  * **Analytical Inference & Unresolved Storyline:** Editor Mags Corliss infers that a growing neighborhood supported by a single listed pantry is *"carrying a lot on a thin frame"* [18]. The unresolved storyline entering Cycle 111 is whether municipal care infrastructure expands to match resident counts in Chinatown and adjacent corridors [18, 23].

---

### **4. 12th Street Is Running Better. The People Are Somewhere Else.**

* **Prior Events & Transit System Dynamics:**  
  * **Cycle 109 Baseline:** Systemwide ridership reached **99,582 boardings** across eight stations [24, 25]. **12th St Oakland City Center Station** logged **23,848 riders** (up 5,472) with an **85% on-time performance rate** [24, 26, 27].  
  * **Cycle 110 Systemwide Shift:** Total 8-station ridership dropped to **91,564 boardings** [28]. **12th St Station** experienced a minor decline of 363 riders while maintaining an **81% on-time rate** [23].  
  * **Cross-Station Divergence:** While 12th St ran steadily, **Lake Merritt Station** suffered the steepest drop, losing 2,588 riders to **5,896 boardings** (84% on-time) [22, 23, 29]. Conversely, **Fruitvale Station** gained 1,321 riders, surging to **11,735 boardings** (78% on-time) [28, 30].  
* **Named Personnel & Staff Witness:**  
  * **Eleanor Rivera** (12th St BART Station Manager): *"It's not just numbers... The team just... adapts"* [24, 26].  
  * **Jerald Jensen** (Janitor): Observed at Lake Merritt that thinner crowds mean *"fewer tips, fewer smiles, fewer connections. It's tough when the lifeblood of a place starts to thin out"* [22, 31].  
  * **Joel Wren** (AC Transit Mechanic) & **Coen Cartier** (Operator): Kept bus and train lines running through rider shifts [24, 25, 32].  
* **Direct Published Facts vs. Inferences:**  
  * **Direct Published Fact:** 12th St Station maintained steady operation (23,485 riders, 81% on-time), while overall system ridership redirected toward Fruitvale (+1,321) and dropped at Lake Merritt (-2,588) [23, 28].  
  * **Analytical Inference & Unresolved Storyline:** Mags Corliss infers that 12th St runs smoothly while rider density moves elsewhere (*"People are going to Fruitvale"*) [30]. The unresolved storyline entering Cycle 111 is how transit planners and operators reallocate resources to match shifting corridor demand [33].

---

### **5. Ellis's Game Five Line Carries the Title**

* **Prior Events & Postseason Performance:**  
  * **John Ellis** pitched a 9-inning complete-game shutout (4 hits, 0 ER, 9 K) in a 4–0 ALDS-closing victory over the Yankees [24, 34, 35].  
  * **Cycle 110 Playoff Mark:** Lead sports reporter **Tanya Cruz** covered the Athletics' clubhouse holding a **4–1 playoff record** [36, 37].  
  * **Danny Horn Dossier:** **Elliot Marbury’s** Data Desk audit confirmed center fielder **Danny Horn's 2041 regular season line** (**56 HRs, 113 RBI, 80 SB, .338 AVG, 1 HR every 11.1 ABs**), noting 1 HR and 2 RBI added in postseason play [36, 38-40].  
* **Named Personnel & Quotes:**  
  * **John Ellis** (Starting Pitcher): Sitting with tape on his fingers, quoted: *"The vibe in here? Electric. We're feeding off each other's energy... pitch by pitch, and trust these guys behind me to keep making plays"* [36, 37].  
  * **Benji Dillon** (Veteran Pitcher): Quoted: *"The clubhouse right now? It's electric, but it's the kind of energy that's grounded... It's not just about talent; it's about trust"* [36, 41].  
  * **Mike Paulson**: General Manager overseeing baseball operations [36, 42].  
* **Direct Published Facts vs. Inferences:**  
  * **Direct Published Fact:** John Ellis leads a 4–1 postseason staff with tape on his fingers, backed by clubhouse trust and chemistry alongside Benji Dillon [36, 37, 41].  
  * **Analytical Inference & Unresolved Storyline:** Tanya Cruz and Mags Corliss question whether clubhouse chemistry holds through the final postseason games [36, 41]. The core unresolved storyline is how John Ellis's Game 5 line and pitching momentum carry the Athletics to the World Series championship under Mike Paulson [36, 37].

### **6. `[suspicious link removed]`**

* **Prior Events & Broadcast Media Impact:**  
  * **Nia Rook** reported from Rockridge on the aftermath of an *UNDOCKED* broadcast featuring **Otis Redd** [43, 44].  
  * **143-Credit Swing:** Otis Redd logged a **143-credit swing** on the night (*"Otis Redd — up 143 on the night"*) [43-45].  
  * **Neighborhood Response:** Sidewalks and living-room screens in Rockridge stayed lit late into the night debating who holds the standings edge [43, 44]. Editor Mags Corliss noted that Rockridge, sitting at the top of the school table, could afford the entertainment [43].  
* **Direct Published Facts vs. Inferences:**  
  * **Direct Published Fact:** Otis Redd gained 143 credits on *UNDOCKED*, sparking widespread debate across Rockridge [43-45].  
  * **Analytical Inference & Unresolved Storyline:** Nia Rook and Corliss infer that television credit swings act as temporary civic amplifiers for local competition [45]. The unresolved storyline entering Cycle 111 is whether Otis Redd's momentum continues to shake up the *UNDOCKED* standings board [45].

references.cited_text: The West Oakland Stabilization Fund, proposed by Mayor Avery Santana and signed into law in Cycle 78 with a 6-3 council vote, is now moving checks through the real machinery of bureaucracy. Cycle 110 marked the ninth month of active disbursement, and the Initiative_Tracker logs the arc: $400,000 approved for Month-Nine, with a 23-day average processing window achieved. The fund's total envelope was $28 million. It has disbursed, in visible tranche, $81,188 in household grants by the end of Cycle 109, and now carries $23 million remaining.

What the tracker shows: a 23-day average processing window in Month Nine. What it does not show, and what no official present offered: how many applications were received, how many were denied, what the demographic footprint of the seventy-nine households looks like, or whether the fund is keeping pace with displacement pressure in the neighborhood or falling behind it. The Finance Committee scrutiny that Webb cited is real—it appears in the Initiative_Tracker as a control gate. The vote itself, in Cycle 78, was narrow: 6-3, with Ramon Vega voting yes, Leonard Tran voting no, and Elliott Crane voting yes remotely. The remaining seats were not named in the record supplied. The fund was designed for West Oakland, the economic policy domain was explicit, and the disbursement phase is active now.

There is also a gap in the arithmetic nobody has explained. The fund was sized at $28 million. Carmen's reporting has about $81,000 in household grants out the door by the end of last cycle, and the same reporting puts the remainder at $23 million. Those figures don't reconcile. Maybe the difference is money committed but not yet paid, or money in another category. Maybe it's a reporting slip. Webb and the Finance Committee can tell us which. Denise Carter said it plainly, "When storefronts go quiet, families go next," and if that's the thesis, residents deserve a clear answer on how much of the money is actually reaching them.

============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic Nine Months, Seventy-Nine Households: The Stabilization Fund Moves at a 23-Day Pace By Carmen Delaine Marcus Webb sat in the Finance Committee chamber with a single line of data that carried the weight of displacement pressure: seventy-nine households stabilized in nine months. He framed the number not as a victory lap but as evidence of traction. "Seventy-nine households stabilized means seventy-nine Oakland families with checks in hand before the displacement notices arrive," Webb said, his tone calibrated to the auditors tracking compliance. Every dollar, he added, moves with the compliance that passes the Finance Committee's scrutiny.

Mayor Santana pressed the speed narrative. "Nine months in, we're proving that relief without bureaucracy keeps neighbors in their neighborhoods," she said in her cycle-110 office record. The claim nested two things: that the mechanism was working, and that other cities or prior efforts had let bureaucracy be the obstacle. Brenda Okoro, in her own statement, refined it further. "Nine months in, the Fund's design is holding—targeted relief that flows to tenants before displacement does," she said. The sequence matters—relief first, displacement second, not the other way around.

The name of the game, as framed by the officials steering it, is speed wrapped in compliance. That friction—moving cash without creating audit liability—is where the story sits this cycle. Denise Carter, City Council District 1, had already staked her position earlier in the cycle on where that friction resolves. "When storefronts go quiet, families go next—so we're taking the Stabilization Fund to where the need is moving," she said. The language was deliberate: the fund is not a static account waiting for applications; it is a tool meant to track and intercept displacement as it moves. The implication was that West Oakland's commercial core and its residential stability are yoked.

THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C109 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ Daniel Cloak was wiping flour off his apron at a West Oakland bakery when he told Carmen Delaine what he thought of the Stabilization Fund. "It feels like something big, but I'm waiting to see it in action." That was the week in one sentence, and it wasn't only West Oakland talking. The fund has passed and money is moving, but as Carmen reported, the people it was built to keep in their homes are still watching. Irene Fay, who pulls morning shifts at a coffee shop nearby, says people are hopeful and skeptical at once. Darius Clark knows exactly what the fund is for and hasn't seen a change on his block. Elena Patel heard about it at the community center last month and still hasn't noticed anything. I don't read that as ingratitude. I read it as people who have watched promises travel slower than they sound.

============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic West Oakland Stabilization Fund Enters Ground Phase—But the Money's Visibility Remains Unclear Daniel Cloak stood behind the counter at the bakery in West Oakland, wiping flour dust from his apron. The morning rush had cleared, and he leaned against the register with the kind of patient skepticism that comes from living in a neighborhood long enough to watch promises move slower than they sound. "I've heard folks talking about the Stabilization Fund at the bakery, but honestly, I'm not sure yet how it's touching the ground here," he said. "It feels like something big, but I'm waiting to see it in action."

That wait—the gap between a fund's official disbursement phase and the moment residents feel its weight on their block—is the ledger's current problem. The West Oakland Stabilization Fund entered its disbursement-active phase this cycle. The Initiative passed. The money is moving through the city's machinery. Yet four weeks into implementation, the people it was built to hold in place remain in the posture of watching. Irene Fay, a barista working the morning shift at a West Oakland coffee shop, had heard the same conversations Cloak tracked at his counter. "I've heard folks at the coffee shop talking about the Stabilization Fund, but honestly, it's hard to tell where that money's actually going. People seem hopeful but also kinda skeptical—like they're waiting to see if it'll really make a difference on our block."

The skepticism is not misplaced. Initiative_Tracker records show the fund's status as passed and active in disbursement phase as of this cycle. That designation means the decision is made and the allocation mechanism is live. It does not yet mean the money has landed in the hands of the people it aims to stabilize—the renters, the long-term residents, the households that have held ground in West Oakland as the city has shifted around them. The fund was designed to keep people in their homes. Darius Clark, another bakery regular in the neighborhood, had absorbed the purpose. "I heard about that fund at the bakery—couple regulars were talking how it's supposed to help keep folks in their homes. Haven't seen much change on my block yet, but I hope it works out."

Elena Patel, a resident, echoed the gap between announcement and arrival. "I heard about the Stabilization Fund at the community center last month, but honestly, I haven't noticed any changes on my block yet." The civic record identifies the Initiative as active in disbursement. The people living under its intended reach report a wait. Neither observation is false. The fund is moving; the ground has not yet shifted. This is the moment where implementation clocks and lived time diverge—where a ledger entry says "phase disbursement-active" and a neighborhood watches for proof.

The next scheduled action is Month-Ten disbursement review in Cycle 111. That checkpoint will show whether the 23-day window holds, whether the pace of cash flow accelerates or stalls, and whether the remaining $23 million carries the same gravity in the tenth month as it did in the ninth. The extraction question Webb's own language raised but could not answer: Are seventy-nine households enough to hold the line in West Oakland's commercial districts before the next wave of displacement notices arrive?

Now set that beside what Jordan Velez found a few blocks over. Oakmesh, Civis Systems and Coastline Construction are all growing along the same West Oakland lane, and the money there is not waiting for anyone. Enzo Walker, a plumber at Oakmesh, told Jordan he spends half his days fixing pipes in buildings that didn't exist last year. "The money's there, sure, but it's not sticking around here." His colleague Dom Will sees the same growth and calls it something real, not a bubble. Sam Fazio at Civis calls it a shared project. Maybe it is. But a neighborhood can have a crane on every corner and a fund in its disbursement phase and still be asking where the help is. Enzo has the quote of the week: "We're all just trying to keep the water running while the city builds over us." Private money arrived fast and visible this week. Public money meant to hold people in place has not yet shown itself. I'd like someone to tell me which of those is outrunning the other.

============================================================ By Jordan Velez | Bay Tribune Business West Oakland’s new business money is moving faster than the block can absorb Enzo Walker spends his working days at Oakmesh Systems keeping water moving through buildings that, in his telling, keep appearing around him. He is a plumber at the West Oakland civic-tech company, working alongside Elijah Roberts, Dom Will and Jace Robinson. Oakmesh, Civis Systems and Coastline Construction are all expanding along the same West Oakland business lane. Those are strong signs. They are also not the same thing as money settling into the neighborhood.

“Honestly? Those tech firms like Oakmesh and Civis—they're changing the block faster than we can keep up. I work at Oakmesh, and half the time I'm fixing pipes in buildings that didn't exist last year. The money's there, sure, but it's not sticking around here. Guys like Elias at Civis talk about 'systems' and 'efficiency,' but ask the folks at the bus stop if they feel any of that. We're all just trying to keep the water running while the city builds over us.” Walker said. The contrast is visible in the roster itself. Oakmesh’s named jobs range from construction labor and plumbing to machine learning. Civis lists Sam Fazio and Catherine Santos as digital twin architects, Elias Varek as founder and Maurice Franklin as drone fleet coordinator. Coastline’s managing partner is Desmond Achebe. Mariner Construction and Northgate Construction are also part of the construction economy around the lane.

Dom Will, a machine learning engineer at Oakmesh, sees the same expansion from inside the company but reads its purpose differently. “Oakmesh feels like we're building something real here - not just another tech bubble. Marcus keeps us focused on civic impact, not just profit. Civis down the street? Elias runs a tight ship, all that urban intelligence work. You see their drone fleet buzzing around sometimes. Coastline's got cranes up everywhere - hard to miss them. But it's the small crews, like our construction guys, that make the neighborhood hum.”

At Civis, Fazio describes the growth as a shared project rather than a balance-sheet story. “Working at Civis Systems, I’ve seen how West Oakland businesses like ours, Oakmesh Systems, and Coastline Construction are really shaping the neighborhood. It’s not just about the jobs—it’s about the community we’re building together. People here are passionate about what they do, whether it’s urban systems intelligence or construction. There’s a sense of pride in contributing to something bigger.” That pride is real in the people carrying the work. So is Walker’s harder question: if the companies are expanding, who gets to feel the benefit beyond the payroll? The next big move for West Oakland’s businesses is not simply whether Oakmesh, Civis Systems or Coastline Construction grows again. It is whether that growth becomes something the block can keep, and who answers for the gap if it does not.

And Maria Keen's piece reminds us who is arriving. Temescal has 311 kids, eight more than last cycle. It has 2,106 working adults, fifty-one more, and 294 seniors, seven more. Nobody is leaving those numbers. Yet the one program of organized care on Maria's block is the Temescal Islamic Center Food Pantry, which has been standing since C83. Omar Lingio loves the fog that settles on his store. Marc Allie and Jackson Sift have both heard, secondhand, about a Temescal Holiday Market. Neither could say where or when. I'd like to know too, and I hope someone with the details calls us. A growing neighborhood with the lowest school index on the table and one pantry holding the line is carrying a lot on a thin frame.

============================================================ By Maria Keen | Bay Tribune Culture Culture — Temescal The sign on Telegraph still says Temescal Islamic Center Food Pantry, same as it did back in C83, when whoever started it first propped a folding table against the wall and called it a program. Twenty-six cycles later it's still the one thing on this block's record that counts as organized care — one program, the ledger says, and for a block this size, carrying this many new faces, that's a thin single line to hang a neighborhood on.

Fog, bassline, a market nobody's confirmed yet — that's the texture holding down a block that's absorbing fifty-plus new adults a cycle on the strength of one listed program. The pantry on Telegraph has been here since C83. Nobody on the ledger can say who started it, who's still running the folding table, or what they'd tell the 311 kids and 2,106 adults now calling this stretch home. That's the name still missing from this block's record. The faces keep coming. Three hundred eleven kids now walk these sidewalks to school, eight more than last cycle. Twenty-one hundred six adults are clocking in somewhere, fifty-one more than before. Two hundred ninety-four seniors are still here too, seven added since C108 — nobody leaving that count, just more joining it. Nobody on the ledger says why they picked this particular stretch of blacktop over another, but ask around Temescal Alley and you get answers anyway, just not the kind that make it into a program file.

Carter's line took on weight when I read Trevor Shimizu's transit reporting. Lake Merritt station lost thousands of riders this cycle, the steepest drop of the eight stations he compared, and its trains ran later than before. Jerald Jensen, who cleans that station, put it in human terms: fewer people means fewer tips, fewer smiles, fewer connections. "The lifeblood of a place starts to thin out." Trevor is careful to say the record points to fog and events but can't tell us which mattered. I'll honor that caution. What I can say is that the quiet is real to the people who work in it.

Lake Merritt moved down more than any other station in the cycle’s eight-station comparison. The change did not arrive with a single reported closure or interruption. The available record identifies fog and events in Lake Merritt and Chinatown, but it does not establish which of those conditions mattered most. The station’s numbers show the result, not the cause. The broader pattern is uneven. MacArthur lost 2,034 riders and fell six points in on-time performance, to 78 percent. Coliseum lost 1,701 riders and fell seven points, to 76 percent. Rockridge lost 1,699 riders and fell three points, to 75 percent. At 19th St Oakland, ridership fell 999 and on-time performance fell seven points, to 79 percent. At 12th St Oakland City Center, the decline was smaller—363 riders—with on-time performance down four points, to 81 percent.

What makes it sharper is Trevor Shimizu's reporting on the trains. Ridership jumped nearly 30 percent across the system, with 99,582 boardings. Fruitvale Station alone logged 10,414, up 3,756. Eleanor Rivera at 12th Street, which took in 23,848 riders, says her team "just adapts." Jerald Jensen, the janitor there, put it more honestly: trash cans overflowing by noon and no time to catch his breath between rushes. Joel Wren, the AC Transit mechanic, credits the crews keeping buses moving. Part of the surge was a game day and a pair of big events at Lake Merritt, so I wouldn't read it as a permanent shift. Still, people are pouring through Fruitvale Station while the hub beside it sits stuck. On-time performance improved, to 85 percent at 12th Street and 81 percent at Fruitvale. The workers are holding the system together. I'd like to see the planners do the same for the lot.

The station isn’t alone. Across Oakland, ridership has jumped nearly 30% this cycle, with 99,582 boardings logged across eight stations and ten corridors. Coliseum Station saw 9,724 riders, a spike of 4,859 from the last cycle, while Fruitvale Station recorded 10,414 boardings, up 3,756. Even MacArthur Station, quieter by comparison, saw a 24% increase, with 12,030 riders passing through its gates. The reasons aren’t hard to spot. Downtown hosted a game day, while Lake Merritt saw two major events. The Baylight District’s ongoing construction planning has also redirected traffic, funneling commuters toward 12th St. Joel Wren, an AC Transit mechanic who works near the station, has noticed the uptick firsthand. “You know, I’ve been seeing more folks hopping on the buses lately—especially down at 12th Street,” Wren says. “It’s good to see people out and about, trusting the system again. But what really gets me is the crew keeping those buses running. Those mechanics and drivers? They’re the ones putting in the long hours to make sure everyone gets where they need to go, especially with all these extra riders.”

============================================================ By Trevor Shimizu | Bay Tribune Civic Ridership Surge at 12th St Oakland City Center Tests Transit Systems At 12th St Oakland City Center, the fares click louder and more often. Eleanor Rivera, a BART station manager, has felt the surge in her bones—23,848 riders this cycle, up 5,472 from the last. “It’s not just numbers,” Rivera says. “It’s people adjusting their routines, and us adjusting right along with them. The team just... adapts. No big announcements, just everyone doing their part to keep things moving smoothly.”

On-time performance has improved at most stations, with 12th St hitting an 85% on-time rate, up four points from the last cycle. Fruitvale Station, despite its own surge, managed an 81% rate, up three points. Even Coliseum Station, often a laggard, saw its rate climb to 83%, up five points. The question now is how long this surge will last—and whether the system can sustain it. It's not just numbers - it's people adjusting their routines, and us adjusting right along with them. The team just... adapts. No big announcements, just everyone doing their part to keep things moving smoothly. | citizenVoice PRESS Eleanor Rivera

But Fruitvale moved in the other direction. It gained 1,321 riders, reaching 11,735, even as on-time performance fell three points to 78 percent. West Oakland gained 45 riders, to 8,680, while its on-time performance fell six points to 75 percent. That split is the important infrastructure fact. The system did not simply become less used everywhere. Across the eight stations and ten corridors measured, total ridership fell to 91,564 from 99,582. The station-level changes point to a network that is carrying different kinds of pressure in different places. Lake Merritt’s decline is the sharpest, but Fruitvale’s increase prevents a clean explanation based only on fog or general movement.

By Trevor Shimizu | Bay Tribune Civic The Quiet at Lake Merritt Is Showing Up in the System By Trevor Shimizu At Lake Merritt station, Jerald Jensen works through a quieter public place. He knows the difference between fog that merely changes the view and a thinner stream of people moving through the station. This cycle, the station recorded 5,896 riders, down 2,588 from the previous cycle. Its on-time performance also slipped, to 84 percent from 86 percent. Jensen, a janitor, said the change is visible beyond the count.

The split in Trevor's numbers is what stayed with me. Fruitvale gained riders, over thirteen hundred of them, even as its trains ran later. West Oakland held roughly steady and its on-time performance dropped six points. People are going to Fruitvale. Which brings me to Luis Navarro's column, and the sentence he caught three officials saying across three cycles. Mayor Santana at the gavel: Mayer & Associates listens to Fruitvale merchants first, designs second. Santana again in open session, nearly word for word. Elena Soria Dominguez on the hub record, with the tamale vendors and panaderías. This cycle Rose Delgado called Phase II's blueprints a "covenant." And the project is still sitting at Visioning, where it has been for three cycles.

“You know, I’ve been hearing chatter about Lake Merritt station being quieter lately. It’s not just the fog—though that doesn’t help. People are talking about how it’s hitting the transit workers hard. Less foot traffic means fewer tips, fewer smiles, fewer connections. It’s tough when the lifeblood of a place starts to thin out.” That is the human reading of a technical condition: fewer riders do not create an empty station, but they alter the work around the trains. The people who clean, direct, serve and maintain a station encounter the system at its edges. A ridership decline becomes fewer brief exchanges, fewer small transactions and fewer reasons for a person to remain in the space.

Jerald Jensen, a janitor at the station, sees the surge in the wear and tear. “More coffee spills to mop up, more trash cans overflowing by noon,” Jensen says. “Used to be you could catch your breath between rushes, but now? It’s constant. Folks pouring in for work, for games, for whatever’s happening downtown.” Coen Cartier, a transit operator, echoes the sentiment. “It’s been busy, but it feels good to know we’re helping people get where they need to go,” Cartier says. “The team’s been working hard to keep things running smoothly, and it’s paying off.”

For workers, the distinction may not make the platform feel less quiet. Jensen’s observation places the cost in the space between the official measures. On-time performance can describe whether service is arriving within its target. Ridership can describe how many people pass through. Neither number captures the social density that Jensen describes: the smiles, tips and connections that make a station more than a transfer point. The next question is operational rather than dramatic. If Lake Merritt’s lower ridership continues, what will distinguish a temporary thinning from a change in how the station is being used? The current numbers show the condition. They do not yet show its duration, its cause or what transit workers will be asked to absorb next.

The numbers seem to tell one story. Eighty-five percent of Temescal students graduate. But only fifty-seven percent test college-ready. That gap—twenty-eight percentage points—sits in the silence between ceremony and consequence. Patricia Nolan, who taught in Temescal for decades before retiring, speaks from the weight of that silence. "After teaching for so many years, I've seen kids walk across that graduation stage who can barely write a proper paragraph," Patricia says. "The numbers might say 85% graduate, but half of them aren't ready for what comes next. It's not just about passing classes—it's about whether these kids can actually think critically when they leave here. We celebrate the diploma, but we're not always honest about what it really means."

The Oakland Unified School District employs 5,201 people citywide and is growing. Temescal's school receives $11,500 in per-student funding—less than Rockridge's $15,000. The city's teacher quality score here sits at 6.96. The question that hangs in the hallway, in the essays, in the families' quiet worry: Is this a resource problem, a culture problem, or something harder to name and fix? DATA DESK: THE HORN LINE Danny Horn's 2041 season carries one number that outranks every other mark on his nine-year dossier: a home run every 11.1 at-bats, worked from a full 621-at-bat season of 148 games. It is the densest power rate the Athletics center fielder has posted in the six seasons for which full lines are on record, and it did not arrive at the cost of swinging more. His strikeout rate that same year — one every 9.6 at-bats — is likewise the loosest of the six, meaning 2041 is the first season in which Horn hit for more power and swung through less at the same time, at a sample size too large to dismiss as a hot month.

Then 2041: 621 at-bats, 210 hits, 56 home runs, 113 runs batted in, 80 stolen bases, a .338 average, an .715 slugging mark. Every rate on the card moved in the same direction at once — more power, fewer empty swings, more hits falling in, more bases taken. No season between 2036 and 2040 approaches that combination at that at-bat count. That is the hard claim the record carries: 2041 sits outside the range Horn established across his previous five recorded seasons, and it did so on a full year's workload, not a partial one.

No peer center fielder's season line is part of this record, so this memo cannot say whether Horn's 2041 density is ordinary or rare for the position this cycle — that comparison is blank here, not answered. The cycle's feed entry adds a small, separate data point: one home run and two runs batted in logged this cycle, in playoff action, with the feed's own notes indicating Horn had struggled across the season before that stretch.
